# Graph `example_graph`

## When to use

Use it for questions about who works where, how the company is structured and who is
accountable for which process. Do not use it for contracts or payroll; those are not in the
graph.

## Is it available here?

Run `graph graphs --json`. Use this skill only if an item named `example_graph` is listed (title: Example graph). Pass `--graph example_graph` to every command, as the examples here do, so they work in every directory; a project whose pointer makes `example_graph` the default may leave it out.

Before your first `graph` command, load the `graph-cli` skill as well: it explains the commands, the output envelope and safe writes. This skill says what the graph holds. Two of its ground rules apply from the first call:

- Run each call as a plain command that starts with `graph`: no `cd`, variables, loops, pipes or heredocs, which a restricted harness refuses. If a call is refused, run it again in that form before you give up.
- For a few fields, a count or a join, use `graph query` and `RETURN` only those columns (read the module first with `graph describe module <module> --graph example_graph`; `graph describe schema --module <module> --graph example_graph --compact --json` lists its patterns), or `--fields <attr>,<attr>` on `find`, `get` and `neighbors`, instead of filtering JSON with another program.

## Subject areas

| Module | Prefix | What it holds | Types | Actions | Links to other modules |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `company` | `co` | The company as a whole, the main module that brings its subject areas together and carries the release of the graph; it holds no terms of its own. | 0 | 0 | none |
| `legal` | `leg` | The legal entities of the group and who owns whom, and which entity employs people or runs units; not the internal structure of the company (organization) or the people (people). | 2 | 0 | `organization` (0 out, 1 in), `people` (1 out, 1 in) |
| `operations` | `ops` | How work gets done, the processes, the instructions and policies that govern them, the trainings roles need and the tasks people carry out; not the structure of the company (organization) or the people (people). | 5 | 1 | `organization` (4 out, 0 in), `people` (1 out, 1 in) |
| `organization` | `org` | The structure of the company, its units, positions, roles and cost centers, and who holds a position; not the people themselves (people) or the work that is done (operations). | 6 | 2 | `legal` (1 out, 0 in), `operations` (0 out, 4 in), `people` (0 out, 1 in) |
| `people` | `ppl` | The people the company works with, employees and externals, and the identities they use in systems; not their positions or units (organization) or their work (operations). | 4 | 1 | `legal` (1 out, 1 in), `operations` (1 out, 1 in), `organization` (1 out, 0 in) |

Built-in modules, shared by every graph: `core`.

- Before you work in a module, read it: `graph describe module <module> --graph example_graph` lists its types, its relations, its links to and from other modules (with the other module named) and its rules. Read its text; `--json` is more than twice the size.
- To find a term whose module you do not know: `graph describe search <text> --graph example_graph --json` (types, relations, fields, enum values and states).
- For the fields, states and relations of one type: `graph describe type <type> --graph example_graph --json`.
- The same module views as text, and an index of every type with its module: [references/model.md](references/model.md) and the pages `references/modules/<module>.md`.

## Changes

Prefer a named action over the single commands when one fits.

4 named actions; for a change use one before you write with the primitives. Dry run first: `graph do <action> --param <name>=<value> --graph example_graph --dry-run`, read what it will change, then run it without `--dry-run`.

- `assign_position(person: ref ppl:Person, position: ref org:Position, since: date)`: Record that a person takes over a position nobody holds, from a date.
- `hand_over_position(position: ref org:Position, person: ref ppl:Person, since?: date)`: Replace the current holder of a position by another person, from a date.
- `offboard_employee(employee: ref ppl:Employee)`: Record that an employee has left; remove their positions and employer first.

More: `graph describe actions --module <module> --graph example_graph`; find one: `graph describe search <text> --kind action --graph example_graph --json`; preconditions and use: `graph describe action <action> --graph example_graph`.

## Names and ids

- Aliases such as `LE-0001` (`leg:LegalEntity`) start with the prefix of the entity's type; the module pages list the prefix of every type, `graph describe type <type> --graph example_graph --json` names it (`alias_prefix`). The number is zero-padded to 4 digits (`LE-0001`, never `LE-1`) and grows past 9999. A full id works everywhere; on the command line 8 or more trailing hex digits of it work too.
- `graph lookup <value> --graph example_graph --json` finds entities by name, ignoring case; it matches the name fields of a type, not other text. The module pages list them per type; `graph describe type <type> --graph example_graph --json` marks them with `role` (`label`: main name; `alt_label`: other names; `hidden_label`: hidden names, matched but never shown).
- Names are not unique, so `lookup` returns candidates; `--for <relation>` or `--for <function>.<param>` keeps those that can fill that slot. Use the returned alias or id only when exactly one candidate matches exactly (`match.kind` is `exact`). With several, or only prefix matches, do not answer about one of them first: unless type and `facts` show which one the request means, list them with their names and ask which one is meant, then answer.
- `graph search <value> --graph example_graph --json` searches names and every text field, forgiving case, accents, typos and parts of words. Its results are suggestions: read one with `graph get` before you use it.
- Before you create an entity of a type with names, search for its name and its short forms. If one is the same thing, use it and add the new name to its other names field instead of creating another. When you create one, fill its other names fields with the abbreviations and synonyms people use. A write finding `data.semantic.possible_duplicate` names entities that already carry the name or a near spelling of it.

## Model

The modules and every type with its module and page: [references/model.md](references/model.md); one page per module in `references/modules/`. Fields, lifecycles and rules of a type, the live source, which wins when they differ: `graph describe type <type> --graph example_graph --json`.
